props.title: I Can't Sleep

sections.content: Claire Denis's haunting **I Can't Sleep (1994)** (1994) weaves together three parallel narratives in Paris, centering on Lithuanian actress Daiga, gay musician Camille, and his brother Theo. The film is loosely based on the true story of Thierry Paulin, known as the "Granny Killer" who terrorized Paris in the 1980s. Denis handles this dark material with remarkable restraint, avoiding sensationalism to create a meditation on urban alienation and immigrant experience. Like her earlier work **Chocolat** (1988), Denis explores colonial legacies and displacement while maintaining an observational distance that heightens the tension.

sections.content: The film's approach to true crime bears comparison to other European art films that deconstruct violence, like **The Vanishing** (1988) and **M** (1931). But Denis's distinctive style - fragmentary, elliptical, focused on bodies and gestures over dialogue - creates a unique atmosphere of creeping dread. The way she captures Paris's multicultural margins recalls **La Haine** (1995), though with a more impressionistic touch. SUBHEAD: Urban Alienation and Identity

Denis's portrayal of marginalized characters navigating Paris speaks to themes that would become even more prominent in French cinema of the 1990s and 2000s. Films like **L'Intrus** (2004) and **Trouble Every Day** (2001) continue her exploration of outsiders and physical displacement. The way **I Can't Sleep** captures the nocturnal rhythm of the city, with its empty streets and isolated figures, creates a portrait of urban loneliness that influenced later works like **Paris** (2008) and 35 Shots of Rum (2008).
